property_summary: After a player loses (random == 0), the reference sends pot - FEE_AMOUNT to the player (i.e., 9 wei), while the buggy version sends pot (i.e., 10 wei). The bank receives 1 wei in both versions, so the divergence is observable via the player's balance after the call.

After a player wins (random == 0) by paying 10 wei, the reference contract correctly transfers 1 wei to bank and 9 wei to the player, leaving 0 balance; the buggy version transfers 10 wei to the player (the entire pot, no fee), so the bank receives no fee, causing address(c).balance to be 0 but the player's balance differs.

After a player loses (random==0), the reference version transfers pot - FEE_AMOUNT to the player and sets pot to 0, while the buggy version transfers the full pot (overpaying the player) and sets pot to 0, resulting in different pot values before the next play.

When the player wins (random == 0), the reference version transfers pot minus FEE_AMOUNT to the player and leaves pot as 0, while the buggy version transfers the full pot (pot) to the player, leaving the bank fee unpaid and pot set to 0. The concrete scenario: one player calls play() with 10 wei, and then after the win, the contract's balance should be 1 wei (the fee) in the reference, but 0 in the buggy version.

After a player calls play{value: 10}(), the reference version deducts a fee from the pot before transferring to the player, while the bug version transfers the full pot (including the fee), causing the player to receive more than intended and bank to receive less.

After a player loses (random == 0), the reference sends the fee to the bank and the pot minus fee to the player, while the buggy version sends the fee to the player and the pot minus fee to the bank, causing the player's balance to differ.

In the reference contract, when player wins (random==0), bank receives FEE_AMOUNT (1 wei) and player receives pot minus fee; in the buggy version, bank receives pot minus fee and player receives only FEE_AMOUNT, so for a play where pot starts at 0 and msg.value=10, reference gives player 9 wei and bank 1 wei, buggy gives player 1 wei and bank 9 wei.

When the reference contract wins (random == 0), the bank receives the fee (1) and the player receives the pot minus the fee (9). In the buggy version, the bank incorrectly receives pot minus fee (9) and the player receives only the fee (1), resulting in different balances for bank and player after a single play.

After the first player wins (random==0), the reference transfers the fee to the bank and the remainder to the player, while the buggy version transfers the fee to the player and remainder to the bank, causing bank balance to be 1 wei higher in the reference for a pot of 10.

After the first player wins, reference sends the winner pot minus fee and bank gets the fee; bug sends winner only the fee and bank gets the rest, thus after a win the reference's bank balance equals 1 and bug's bank balance equals 9.

When the random outcome is 0, the reference version sends the pot (minus fee) to the player and resets pot to 0, while the buggy version (random == 1) does nothing, leaving pot unchanged after the call.

After a player sends 10 wei to play() and wins (random == 0), the reference contract sets pot to 0 and sends 9 wei to the player; the buggy version only sends funds when random == 1, so the player's 10 wei remain in the pot and the bank never gets the fee.

After two players each pay the ticket amount, the pot doubles and one play (with random == 0 in reference / random == 1 in bug) pays the bank fee and transfers the remainder to the player. In the reference, random == 0 triggers the payout; in the bug, random == 1 triggers it, so with a block hash that gives random == 0 the reference pays out and the bug does nothing, making the bank's balance 1 in reference and 0 in bug.

After the first player plays and wins (random==0), the reference contract sends the pot minus fee and resets pot to 0; the buggy contract does nothing on random==1, so pot remains 10 and bank never receives fee. Then a second player playing again triggers the buggy contract to incorrectly add another 10 to pot and on random==0 send a larger amount (20-1=19) to the second player, while the reference correctly sends 10-1=9 and resets pot.

After a player sends 10 wei to play(), the reference contract transfers the pot minus fee (9 wei) when random == 0, whereas the buggy contract does so when random == 1, resulting in zero balance for the player for this concrete block where random == 0.

After a player wins (random == 0), the reference contract sends pot minus fee to the player and resets pot to 0; the buggy contract always sends pot minus fee and resets pot to 0 even when random == 1, so after losing the buggy version incorrectly transfers funds and resets pot while the reference does nothing.

After one player wins the lottery (random == 0), the reference sets pot to 0, but the buggy version always transfers and resets pot (even when random != 0), so the buggy version always leaves pot = 0 after any play call, while the reference leaves pot unchanged on a loss.

After one play call that loses (random == 1), the reference leaves pot unchanged (10) and does not send the fee, while the buggy version in the else branch sends the fee and resets pot to 0, so c.pot() diverges: reference returns 10, buggy returns 0.

After two calls to play() with equal Ether sent to the contract, the reference contract resets pot to 0 only when random==0 and does not send funds on random==1, so pot accumulates; the buggy version always clears pot and sends funds, making pot always 0 after each call.

After one player sends 10 wei, if random is 1, the reference leaves pot unchanged (10) and bank + player balances untouched for the losing player; the buggy version sends all pot minus fee to bank and player anyway, leaving pot = 0 and changing balances.
After two calls to play(), when both calls lose (random==0), the reference version resets pot to zero, while the buggy version does not reset pot, causing address(c).balance to differ.
The reference contract resets pot to 0 after a win, whereas the buggy version does not reset pot, so after a winning play, address(c).balance differs.
After one play() call that wins (random == 0), the pot in the reference version is reset to 0, while in the buggy version pot remains unchanged (still 10).

When a player wins (random == 0), the reference version sets pot = 0, but the buggy version does not; after a win, reading c.pot() returns 0 in the reference but retains the pot value minus fee in the buggy version.

After two plays where the first player wins and resets pot to 0, the reference contract retains 1 wei as bank fee from the winner's payout, while the buggy contract does not transfer the fee, leaving pot unchanged at 10, so address(c).balance differs.

After a player wins (random==0), the reference version sets pot to 0 and the player receives pot minus fee, while the buggy version sets pot to 0 immediately after the if block regardless of win/loss, but for a win scenario the pot is already 0 before the transfer so the player gets less Ether (transfer of 0) causing c.pot() to be 0 in both versions but address(c).balance differs: reference leaves pot fee (1 wei) in the contract, buggy leaves nothing.
After a play() call where random == 1 (lose), the reference version keeps the pot as accumulated (10) while the buggy version resets the pot to 0.

After play() is called by a user with 10 wei when random==0, the reference version keeps pot=0; the buggy version sets pot=0 again, which is the same, but if the second call is from a user who loses (random==1), the reference keeps pot equal to the accumulated amount (10 wei from the first call) while the buggy version prematurely zeros it before the if, causing pot=0 after both calls.
After a win (random == 0), the reference contract sets pot = 0, while the buggy version adds an extra unconditional fee transfer and does not reset pot, causing pot to be non-zero.

In the reference version, after a player wins (random == 0), the pot is reset to 0; in the modified version, an additional fee transfer after the if-block occurs even when the player won, which will revert due to insufficient balance if bank address is a contract that rejects ether, causing the transaction to fail. The test uses a non-payable actor as bank by exploiting that the constructor sets bank = msg.sender, then uses a different caller to play so that the bank is a non-payable address; after a win, in the reference the call succeeds, in the buggy version it reverts.

After a winning play (random==0) that resets pot to 0, the modified version transfers an extra FEE_AMOUNT to bank, changing address(c).balance from 9 to 10, while the reference leaves pot=0 and address(c).balance=9.

After a single play() call from an address where random == 0, the reference contract resets pot to 0 and sends the balance minus fee to the player, so player ends with address(this).balance == initial + pot - FEE_AMOUNT - fee; the bug version always sends an extra FEE_AMOUNT to bank unconditionally after the if block, draining the contract's ether and making the player's balance unchanged, causing bank's balance to differ.

After a player wins (random == 0), the reference contract resets pot to 0 and sends pot - FEE_AMOUNT to the player and FEE_AMOUNT to the bank; the buggy version sends an extra FEE_AMOUNT to the bank after the if block, so the bank's balance becomes 2*FEE_AMOUNT instead of FEE_AMOUNT.

Alice sends exactly 10 wei to play(); the reference contract accepts it and updates pot, while the buggy contract also accepts it but the assertion checks that the pot after the call equals 10, which holds for the reference but fails for the buggy version because the require statement uses >= instead of ==, allowing different amounts.

After the first player sends exactly 10 wei and wins, the reference contract sets pot to 0, so a second player sending 10 wei will have pot equal to 10 before the random check; the buggy contract allows a player to send more than 10 wei, so after a first win, a second player sending 20 wei can cause pot to be >10 and the bank fee transfer might fail due to insufficient balance.

After a player sends exactly 10 wei (the TICKET_AMOUNT) and wins (random == 0), the bank receives a 1 wei fee and the player receives the pot minus fee; the reference requires msg.value == 10, while the bug requires msg.value >= 10, so a player sending 11 wei wins and the pot becomes 22 wei (instead of 20) leading to different balances — the assertion checks that after the win, bank.balance is 1 wei (fee) in the reference but 1 wei in the bug as well? Actually we want a divergence: we send 10 wei to win, both behave same; to diverge send 11 wei; bug accepts, reference reverts. So test: player sends 11 wei, reference reverts (assertTrue(!ok) for the reference), bug does not revert (ok true) and bank gets 1 fee, pot becomes 0, player gets 10? Actually pot += 11 => 11, then fee 1 sent, player gets 10, pot=0. So bank.balance is 1. For reference, the call reverts (msg.value == 10 fails). Thus we assert that reference call reverts but bug call succeeds.

After one player calls play() and loses (random == 0), the pot is zero and the bank receives the fee; in the buggy version pot = msg.value resets the pot to 10 instead of accumulating, so after the bank fee and player payout, pot is not zeroed correctly but the final pot value (0) is the same as reference; however, the bug is that the bank receives 1 fee (same) but the player payout is pot - FEE_AMOUNT which in reference is (10 - 1) = 9, and in buggy pot is overwritten to 10 so payout is 9 as well due to the subsequent calculation; actually both give same payout. Need a scenario where pot is accumulated across calls: first player loses (pot = 0), second player calls play and wins, so bank gets fee and player gets pot - fee; in reference pot was 10 from second call? Wait, the bug is that the buggy version sets pot = msg.value instead of pot += msg.value, so if a prior call left pot at 0, the second call adds only msg.value in reference but in buggy it resets to msg.value, so the final pot after second call before win/loss is same? Actually after first loss, pot is set to 0 in both versions because the if block resets pot = 0. For the second call, reference does pot += 10 => pot = 10, buggy does pot = 10 => pot = 10, so same. To see divergence, the player must win: in reference pot becomes pot += msg.value = 10, then player wins so pot stays? Wait win condition is random == 0? Actually code: if (random == 0) { fee transfer, player transfer, pot = 0; }. So win means pot distributes and zeroes. Loss means nothing happens, pot retains its value. So scenario: first player plays and loses (random != 0) — pot accumulates. Second player plays and loses again — pot accumulates. In reference, pot becomes 20; in buggy, pot becomes 10 (overwritten). Then third player plays and wins — in reference, pot = 20, bank gets 1, player gets 19, pot becomes 0. In buggy, pot = 10, bank gets 1, player gets 9, pot becomes 0. The bank balance after the winning call: in reference bank receives 1, in buggy bank receives 1 (same for that call). But the player balances differ. However, to test we can observe c.pot() after the second call but before the third: reference pot = 20, buggy pot = 10. So assertEq(c.pot(), 20) after two losses passes on reference, fails on buggy.
